comment: The Ministry supports treating interoperability as a structural property rather than a later integration exercise. The principle as drafted, however, addresses only one of the two ways a health system achieves it. Its whole substance concerns the topology of exchange — centralised mediator versus distributed capability, federated access, connectivity assumptions. Interoperability achieved at the data layer, where contributing systems write to and read from a shared, governed record rather than exchanging between themselves, is not distinguished from application-to-application exchange at all. The phrase "common data models" appears once, at line 244, undefined and unconnected to the Logical Information Model Repository that section 3.6.2 identifies as governing structure. In Slovenia's experience the distinction is the most consequential one a country makes: where contributing systems conform to one governed record, the number of interfaces to be built, tested and maintained falls with each system added rather than rising, and much of the exchange burden the principle discusses does not arise.

public.text: The Ministry supports treating interoperability as a structural property rather than a later integration exercise. The principle as drafted, however, addresses only one of the two ways a health system achieves it. Its whole substance concerns the topology of exchange — centralised mediator versus distributed capability, federated access, connectivity assumptions. Interoperability achieved at the data layer, where contributing systems write to and read from a shared, governed record rather than exchanging between themselves, is not distinguished from application-to-application exchange at all. The phrase "common data models" appears once, at line 244, undefined and unconnected to the Logical Information Model Repository that section 3.6.2 identifies as governing structure. In Slovenia's experience the distinction is the most consequential one a country makes: where contributing systems conform to one governed record, the number of interfaces to be built, tested and maintained falls with each system added rather than rising, and much of the exchange burden the principle discusses does not arise.
public.suggestedRevision: Add after line 244: "Interoperability is achieved in two ways, and countries should be explicit about which they are relying on for a given flow. Data-level integration, in which contributing systems write to and read from a shared record governed by a common information model, removes the need for exchange between those systems. Exchange-level integration, in which systems that hold their own data communicate through standardised services, remains necessary across organisational and national boundaries. The first reduces the number of interfaces a country must build and maintain; the second cannot be avoided entirely. The design question is which flows belong in which category."
